# Uragajātaka (Ja 354)

**ID:** Ja 354
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Uragajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Snake
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja354
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul4.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Uragajātaka* (Ja 354) is a canonical birth-story in the Jātaka collection of the Khuddaka Nikāya [SuttaCentral]. The Buddha delivered the story at Jetavana to console a grieving landowner whose son had recently died, an occasion paralleling similar discourses delivered to bereaved persons [SuttaCentral; Burlingame 1921; Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. The Buddha admonishes the layman that death is universal and urges him to emulate the wise figures of the past who engaged in mindfulness of death rather than giving way to sorrow [Burlingame 1921]. In the narrative of the past, the Bodhisatta lived as a householder who exhorted his household—including his wife, identified in the Buddhist tradition as an earlier rebirth of the nun Khemā—to practice generosity, maintain the precepts, observe the uposatha, and constantly reflect on mortality [Nyanaponika et al. 2003].

When the Bodhisatta's son is fatally bitten by a snake while clearing fields, the Bodhisatta remains composed, continues his work, and imparts a discourse on impermanence (*anicca*) to a neighbor [UNDV Conference Volume 2009; Söhnen-Thieme]. The central verse teaching employs the metaphor of a snake shedding its skin: just as a serpent sloughs off its old skin without attachment, a human spirit abandons its physical corpse, which is insensible to the lamentations of kin [Burlingame 1921; Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. This narrative motif is also preserved in traditional Sinhalese temple art, such as murals at Madawala Vihāra depicting the field scene amidst rich botanical landscapes [UNDV Conference Volume 2009]. Söhnen-Thieme notes a remote parallel to this episode in the *Mahābhārata*, though the epic reorients the story away from the Buddhist family's stoic equanimity [Söhnen-Thieme].

Curated cross-references and text-reuse alignments demonstrate that the *Uragajātaka* corresponds directly to the *Uragapetavatthu* (Pv 12) [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus; Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. DharmaNexus records substantial verse-level identity between Ja 354 and Pv 12 (§0.3–11.1 ↔ §0.2–11.1), as well as extensive reuse across exegetical literature, including the *Petavatthu-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, and the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus], the last of which quotes the verses in full when narrating the Buddha's consolation of the grieving layman [Burlingame 1921].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Mentioned in (SuttaCentral): Pv 12 Uragapetavatthu
- Text reuse within the Pali corpus (DharmaNexus): Petavatthu-aṭṭhakathā (Atk S0507a) (§4.4–6.4 ↔ §498_2–504); Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā (Tatiyo bhāgo) (Atk S0513a3) (§4.4–6.4 ↔ §1386_2–1392); Uragapetavatthu (Pv 12) (§0.3–11.1 ↔ §0.2–11.1); Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā (Atk S0502a) (§1.1–2.4 ↔ §3127–3130)

- [DharmaNexus] DharmaNexus computed parallels — Provides algorithmic text-reuse alignments with Pv 12, Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā, Petavatthu-aṭṭhakathā, and Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā.
- [UNDV Conference Volume 2009] UNDV Conference Volume, Buddhist Approach to Environmental Crisis (2009) — Describes the narrative plot of the son bitten by a snake, the teaching on impermanence, and temple murals at Madawala Vihara.
- [Burlingame 1921] Eugene W. Burlingame, Buddhist Legends: Translated from the Original Pali Text of the Dhammapada Commentary (1921) — Details the Dhammapada commentary's use of the Uraga Jātaka and provides translations of the core snake-skin verses.

- [Söhnen-Thieme] Renate Söhnen-Thieme, Buddhist tales in the Mahābhārata — Discusses the Mahabharata parallel to the snake-bite story and its divergence from the Jātaka's stoic theme.
